title: Story Divider
context: Grade 4, and the topic where division stops being given as a division. An adult sees word problems. What is actually being taught is deciding: which number is the total being shared, which is the number of equal parts, and which part of the answer each question wants. The worked example that finds a missing factor brings two digits down together in its figure and never shows the step that puts the zero in two hundred and three, and without that step the answer reads twenty-three. The exercise that follows ends on two questions that each ask what is left, and there the remainder is an answer and not a leftover to be dropped.

writeup.why: Read a story, decide what is shared and into how many, and give every part of the answer the question asks for.
writeup.look: A story card at the top with its numbers lit, two slots and a share bar under it, a division frame beside them and an answer builder at the right.
writeup.stage: Three bands across 1600 by 900. The header runs 0 to 80 and is one line only: 'Story Divider' in ink at the far left, a small dot set clear of the name by measuring it, the phase title beside the dot on the same line, the host's navigation, and again, sound and restart as three round controls at the far right. The canvas runs 92 to 746, one rounded card on the paper colour. At its top left, at 64,108 and 330 by 76, sits the running count: the asks answered against the asks this question makes, two numbers in ink, the first climbing by one as each slot of the answer builder fills with its number and its unit, and the second fixed at how many things the question asks. Nothing in it ever counts down and nothing in it ever reads as a score. The working area is 1086 by 528 at 64,202. The story card runs across the top of the working area, 1086 by 110 at 64,210, holding the story in large type with each of its numbers lit, deep blue for the total and amber for the parts once each job is found and plain ink until then. Under it the total slot, 250 by 70 at 64,336, and the parts slot, 250 by 70 at 334,336, take a number dragged from the story; a number dropped in the slot whose job it does not do in this story springs back while the words of the story that name that job are lit, nothing marked. Once both are filled the share bar is drawn under them, 520 by 64 at 64,426, in deep blue, split into as many equal parts as the parts slot says, every part genuinely the same length, and one part lights green when its size is found. The missing factor bay sits under the bar, 520 by 200 at 64,510, three boxes for the product and its two numbers, with a line under them that multiplies the two numbers back to the product. The division frame stands to the right, 480 by 390 at 640,336, with its place headings, and its bring down arrow brings one digit at a time: a second digit dragged down with the first springs back to its place, so a step where the number is smaller than the divisor is always shown and its grey zero written in the quotient. Down the right of the canvas, in the same rectangle on every phase and never animated in or out, the question sits above the answer slot at 1186,250 (356 by 92) that holds what the child has given, and under it the pad at 1170,368 (388 by 363). The pad is twelve number keys three across wherever a number is asked for, with a unit strip under it, kilometres, litres, millilitres, minutes, trees, cars, tiles, children and centimetres among them, because every slot of the answer builder takes a unit as well as a number. The footer runs 758 to 900: the voice caption at the far left with its speaking dot beside it, measuring its own wrap and dropping a type size rather than spilling, and the phase bar at the right with the question count under it. There is no sidebar and no score box anywhere, and nothing is ever written over the working area. Content colours are the chapter's own: the dividend, the whole being shared and any total, is deep blue; the divisor, and the plates, groups or envelopes it makes, is amber; the quotient and each equal share are green; what is left over, at one step or at the end, is vermilion; a multiple of the divisor, tried on a ladder or taken away as a chunk, is rose; and a zero written in the quotient because the number was smaller than the divisor is grey. Chrome never borrows one of those and none of them is ever used for chrome. Every reading survives with the colour taken away, because what is left over is told by the dish or the slot it sits in, a quotient digit by the row it sits in, and a multiple by the rung or the column that holds it, before any of them is told by a colour, and every rule, bracket, cell edge and guide line is near-black. Grey never means faint: a zero in the quotient is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit and is never dimmed, shrunk or left out. The answer slot on the right is the answer builder on this tool. It splits into one row for each thing the question asks, each row with its unit written after the box, and it closes only when every row is filled. The quotient and the remainder are never put in one row, so a question that asks what is left shows its second row waiting from the first frame.
writeup.finish: The card shows the last story the child worked, its share bar split into equal parts, and every slot of the answer builder filled with its unit.

phases.win: the bar splits into equal parts and one part's size lands in the answer builder
phases.does: drags each number from the story into the slot for the job it does, then reads the share bar
phases.goal: the total being shared is the dividend and the number of equal parts is the divisor
phases.says: Which number is being shared out? Into how many equal parts?
phases.check: Seventy-two chairs are set out in six equal rows. Point to the total and the parts, then say how many chairs are in a row.
phases.feels: the story decides which number is the whole, and the words that decide it can be pointed to
phases.hands: Read a sharing story aloud with two numbers in it, and have the class say which number is the whole amount and which is the number of equal parts, pointing to the words that told them. Then read one where the whole amount comes last in the sentence, and ask whether the order of the words changed which number is shared.
phases.tries: A miss is answered three ways at once and none of them is the answer. First rung, from the item's own miss line: what is the whole amount in this story? Second rung, the phase's: which words say how many equal parts? Third rung: the story is cut to twelve apples in three bags, and the child fills both slots from it. The number pad and the unit strip stay open behind all three rungs.

wrong.why: both numbers are in the story and a division needs one on each side, so either order can feel like a division of the story.
wrong.move: divides the petrol by the distance, which asks how much petrol one kilometre takes, a different question from the one set.
wrong.screen: the child's twenty-four springs back out of the total slot while the words for the whole trip are lit, and the child's order is drawn as a second bar beside the story's: the petrol cut into four hundred and fifty-six parts, each far less than a litre, beside the distance cut into twenty-four equal parts of nineteen kilometres. Both bars stay drawn, nothing marked.

wrong.why: the last word said in the division was litres, and the unit of the number divided by is the one still in the ear.
wrong.move: finds nineteen and writes it as litres, when the question asked how far the van goes.
wrong.screen: the answer builder's row carries the unit the question asks for, kilometres, written after the box, and the child's litres is laid beside it. The share bar is then read part by part, each part a stretch of road nineteen kilometres long with the one litre it used drawn under it.

phases.screen: a story card with two numbers lit and the total and parts slots empty
phases.soWhat: The total being shared is the dividend and the number of equal parts is the divisor.
phases.concept: What is shared, and into how many

phases.win: the missing number settles and the two numbers multiply back to the product
phases.does: divides the product by the known number, then multiplies back to check
phases.goal: a missing factor is the product divided by the factor that is known
phases.says: You know the product and one number. How do you find the other?
phases.check: Two numbers multiply to make nine hundred and twelve, and one of them is twenty-four. Find the other, then multiply back.
phases.feels: a product and one of its numbers are a division waiting to be done, and multiplying back says whether it was done right
phases.hands: Draw a rectangle of dots, seven rows of eight, and cover all but one row with a sheet of paper. Tell the class how many dots there are altogether and how many are in the row they can see, and ask how many rows are hidden. Then lift the sheet and count.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: which number is the product? Second rung, the phase's: what do you do to the product with the number you know? Third rung: the bay is cut to a product of fifty-six with one number seven, and the child finds the other and multiplies back. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the word product is the word for multiplying, and it sits in the question beside two numbers.
wrong.move: multiplies the two numbers given, as if the product were one of the factors.
wrong.screen: the bay writes the child's number, ninety-four thousand two hundred and eight, in the empty box and multiplies it back by thirty-two, which lands nowhere near two thousand nine hundred and forty-four. The bay then divides the product by the number that is known, writes ninety-two, and multiplies the two back to the product exactly, with the child's number still standing above.

wrong.why: the division felt like the whole job, and the product in the question looks like something already used up.
wrong.move: writes ninety-one after a slip at the last step, and never multiplies back to see it.
wrong.screen: the bay multiplies thirty-two by ninety-one and writes two thousand nine hundred and twelve under the product, exactly one thirty-two short. The child's ninety-one stays in its box, and the last step is replayed in the frame, sixty-four ones holding two thirty-twos.

phases.screen: the missing factor bay holding a product and one of its two numbers
phases.soWhat: A missing factor is the product divided by the factor that is known.

phases.win: the zero lands in its place and the answer reads with every digit it needs
phases.does: brings down one digit only, sees it is smaller than the divisor, writes the zero, then brings the next
phases.goal: a zero goes in the quotient when the number brought down is smaller than the divisor, and one digit at a time shows it
phases.says: Bring down one digit only. How many fit into that?
phases.check: Divide six thousand one hundred and eighty by thirty, one digit at a time. Where does the zero go, and why?
phases.feels: the step that gives nothing is still a step, and it has to be written down or the answer loses a place
phases.hands: Work five thousand and seventy-five divided by twenty-five on the board, the chapter's own missing factor example, bringing down one digit only at each step. When the seven comes down alone, ask how many twenty-fives fit into seven tens, and write the zero. Then bring the five down and finish, and ask what the answer would read without the zero.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many digits did you bring down? Second rung, the phase's: is the number now being divided smaller than the divisor? Third rung: the frame is cut to a three-digit dividend with one hidden zero, and the child brings the digits down one by one. The number pad stays open.

wrong.why: the chapter's own figure for this idea brings two digits down at once, and the number they make is one the divisor fits, so nothing seems to have been skipped.
wrong.move: brings two digits down together and loses the zero, so two hundred and seven is read as twenty-seven.
wrong.screen: the frame sends the second digit back to its place and brings down the six alone: sixteen tens, laid against twenty-four, falls short, because sixteen is smaller than twenty-four, and the grey zero drops into the tens place. The eight then comes down. The check multiplies twenty-four by the child's twenty-seven, six hundred and forty-eight, far short of the dividend, while two hundred and seven rebuilds it exactly.

wrong.why: a step that gives nothing feels like a step that used everything up, and the zero looks like the end of those tens.
wrong.move: writes the zero for sixteen tens and then divides the eight on its own, as if the sixteen tens had gone.
wrong.screen: what is left under the zero step, sixteen tens, stays lit in the frame, still there, and the bring down arrow lays the eight beside it, so the working number reads one hundred and sixty-eight ones. The child's eight ones stay written above it, and seven twenty-fours are laid against the larger number and fit it exactly.

phases.screen: a frame where the next number to divide will be smaller than the divisor, with two digits waiting
phases.soWhat: A zero goes in the quotient when the number brought down is smaller than the divisor, and one digit at a time shows it.

phases.win: both slots fill with their units and the answer closes
phases.does: works the division, puts the quotient in one slot and the remainder in the other, each with its unit
phases.goal: when a question asks what is left, the remainder is part of the answer
phases.says: The question asks two things. Which part of the division answers each?
phases.check: Nine hundred and fifty-eight marbles go equally into forty bags. How many go in each bag, and how many are left? Give both with units.
phases.feels: the leftover is not waste this time, it is the answer to half the question
phases.hands: Plan a trip for the class on paper: how many children, and how many seats in a van. Work out how many full vans there are and how many children are left over. Then ask two questions, how many full vans and how many children are left, and let the class say which part of the division answers each.
phases.tries: First rung, from the item: how many things does the question ask? Second rung, the phase's: which part of the division answers each one? Third rung: the answer builder is cut to its two rows with the quotient already in the first, and the child fills only the second. The number pad and the unit strip stay open.

wrong.why: the quotient is the number the division was worked to find, and a leftover has always been something to set aside.
wrong.move: gives only three hundred and thirteen and drops the ten millilitres, which answers the second question.
wrong.screen: the answer builder stays open with its second row lit and empty, its unit, millilitres, already written after it, and the running count reads one ask answered of two. The remainder is lifted from the foot of the frame, where it has stood the whole time, and carried across to that row, with the child's first row left exactly as it was filled.

wrong.why: the divisor was bowls and the last unit said aloud was bowls, so the leftover borrows it.
wrong.move: gives the remainder the unit of the parts, ten bowls left over instead of ten millilitres.
wrong.screen: the unit strip lights millilitres against the row, and the share bar is read again: fifteen bowls each holding three hundred and thirteen millilitres, and ten millilitres of soup drawn apart from them in a dish of its own, soup and not bowls. The child's row keeps its number and its unit until the child changes it.

phases.screen: a story that asks two things, with two slots open in the answer builder
phases.soWhat: When a question asks what is left, the remainder is part of the answer.
phases.concept: When the leftover is part of the answer

writeup.delight: The third phase, when one digit comes down at a time. The seven tens drop into the working number alone, twenty-five is laid against them and they fall short, and a grey zero drops into the tens place of the quotient at full size. Then the five comes down to join the seven, making seventy-five ones, and the last digit settles. Beside it a copy of the frame brings the two digits down together at the same moment, ends one digit short, and reads twenty-three against two hundred and three, both left standing. It runs as often as a finger likes, nothing is marked, and the voice says nothing at all while it happens.
writeup.opening: Every mount comes up already furnished for its phase with nothing in front of it. On the first phase a story card stands across the top with two numbers lit, the total slot and the parts slot empty under it and no bar drawn yet. On the second the missing factor bay holds a product and one of its two numbers, with the third box empty. On the third a division stands part way in the frame, the next number to divide is going to be smaller than the divisor, and two digits wait above the frame to come down. On the fourth a story that asks two things stands on the card, and the answer builder down the right has two slots open, each with its unit already written after it. The running count at the top left holds the asks answered against the asks the question makes, and the pad stands empty down the right. One thing moves, once: the first lit number, or the empty box, or the next digit waiting, or the second empty slot, gives one slow pulse while the voice asks which number is being shared. That pulse is the only invitation, and a finger on it is the whole way in.
writeup.freePlay: Any story card, with the missing factor bay, the frame and the answer builder open. Nothing to get right, no target and no timer. The child is left with the same stage and every control unlocked.
writeup.practice: Eight items over the four phases, easy first, on deciding what is shared and into how many, finding a missing factor, catching a hidden zero, and giving the remainder when the question asks what is left.

observations.why: Which number is the total depends on what the story says, not on which number comes first.
observations.soWhat: Find the total being shared and the number of equal parts from the words, before dividing.
observations.observe: A number dropped in the parts slot sprang back while the story's words for the parts lit up.

observations.why: A product divided by one of its two numbers leaves the other.
observations.soWhat: A missing factor is the product divided by the factor that is known.
observations.observe: The missing number was found by dividing, and the two numbers multiplied back to the product.

observations.why: Seven tens is smaller than twenty-five, so that step puts a zero in the quotient, and bringing two digits down together skips it.
observations.soWhat: Without that zero, two hundred and three reads twenty-three, so every step is shown one digit at a time.
observations.observe: Bringing down one digit at a time showed a step that bringing two together had hidden.

observations.why: The question asked two things, and the remainder is the answer to one of them.
observations.soWhat: When a question asks what is left, the remainder is part of the answer, with its unit.
observations.observe: The answer would not close while the row for what was left stood empty.

source_tool.description: A story card sits at the top of the stage with its numbers lit. Two slots wait under it, one for the total being shared and one for the number of equal parts, and a number dragged from the story settles only in the slot whose job it does in that story; a total dropped in the parts slot springs back with the story's wording for the parts lit. Once both are in, a bar for the total is drawn and split into that many equal parts, and the division runs in a frame beside it. A missing factor bay holds a product and one of its two numbers and builds the other by dividing. The frame brings digits down one at a time and refuses a pair brought down together, so every step shows, including the one where the number is smaller than the divisor and a zero goes in the quotient. An answer builder at the right lists what the question asks, one slot to each ask and each slot carrying the unit the question uses, so a question asking how many in each and how many are left needs both the quotient and the remainder before it closes.
source_tool.art_direction: A story card over a share bar / Picture book

stage.furniture: The working area is furnished from the first frame. What waits for the child is the count, not the picture: the panels, the slot and the pad are all up and empty before anything is asked.
stage.noSidebar: There is no sidebar. The canvas takes every unit the chrome can spare, because the working area is the tool.
stage.noScoreBox: There is no score box anywhere on the stage. The score leaves on the finished event and it is the host that decides whether to show it, so a child working is never watching a number that judges them.

style.motion: Animate only what carries meaning. Anything that is not changing does not move. Every reward is the maths itself moving, never confetti. Honour prefers-reduced-motion.
drawing: Hand-built inline SVG. No assets and no network, so a school cart works offline.
Chunky rounded forms and large touch targets. A finger is the pointer, not a mouse.

Drawn things, not abstract boxes: a tray of counters and a row of plates, digit cards under place headings, sticks tied in bundles, a long division frame with its bracket, a ladder of multiples, a strip of cells, a story card, and two rails tied at every stop.

Equal shares are drawn genuinely equal and genuinely countable. Where a plate or a part is labelled with a number, exactly that many things are on it, and anything counted one at a time is drawn in rows of ten so that no more than twenty loose things ever have to be counted singly.

What is left over is drawn OUTSIDE the shares, in a dish or a slot of its own, at full strength and fully countable. It is never faded, never tucked under a share and never left to be guessed from a gap.
A division is always written with every place headed. The number being divided at a step is shown with its place name, so fifteen tens is never drawn as a bare fifteen.

Every zero in a quotient is drawn at the same size and weight as the other digits and is never dimmed, shrunk or dropped. A zero is written only where the number being divided is smaller than the divisor, and a leading zero may stand or be left off, but a zero after the first digit always stands.
What is left at every step is drawn in its own slot before the next digit comes down, and it slides down to join that digit so the next number can be seen being made.
A remainder is written as a number. A zero standing in front of its other digits is lifted off and set aside, never written into the answer.
No stage ever shows a number for a division by zero. Where one is asked, the stage says it is not possible and draws nothing to share into.
Two answers being compared stand on the stage at the same time, one beside or above the other. An answer that has been replaced is never cleared away.
style.palette_rule: A chrome colour never fills a counter, a digit or a card the child is reading, and a content colour is never used for chrome. These are the chapter's own colours, so a tool and a picture of the same thing are the same colour. The dividend, the whole being shared and any total, is deep blue; the divisor, and the plates, groups or envelopes it makes, is amber; the quotient and each equal share are green; and what is left over, at one step or at the end, is vermilion. Those four hold from the plates to the frame to the story card in every tool of this chapter. A multiple of the divisor, whether it is being tried on the ladder or taken away as a chunk, is rose, so the chunks can be added up without being mistaken for the share. A zero written in the quotient because the number was smaller than the divisor is grey, and grey never means faint: it is drawn at the same size and weight as every other digit, because it is holding a place. All of that holds in greyscale, because what is left over is told apart by the dish or the left slot it sits in, and a quotient digit by the row it sits in, before either is told apart by colour.

rules: Every spoken line is also printed in the caption line at the far left of the footer, so a muted tablet and a child who cannot hear lose nothing.
The caption stays in the footer. Nothing is ever written over the working area.

Numbers are written as words in every line and never as digits, so the voice says four steps and not 4 steps. Handed a digit, a synthesiser reads it in whatever register it likes and the chapter loses the words it is teaching.
The voice never gives the answer. It asks the same question a different way.
It speaks on opening, once when a phase begins, on a miss, and at the finish. It is silent otherwise; a tool that chatters gets muted, and then the first rule is all that is left.

placement.where: After a class has planned a trip on paper, working out how many full vans the class fills and how many children are left over. The tool is what refuses to close an answer while one of the question's asks is still empty, which a single answer line on paper never does.

answer_key.rule: In a word problem, the total being shared is the dividend and the number of equal parts is the divisor. The answer to how many in each is the quotient. When two numbers multiply to make a product and one of them is known, the other is the product divided by the one that is known. Bring down one digit at a time, because a zero goes in the quotient whenever the number being divided is smaller than the divisor, and bringing two digits down together hides that step. When a question asks how many are left, the remainder is part of the answer and must be given. Answers carry the unit the question uses. Where a question shares a time or an amount out and asks for each part, each part is the same time or the same amount, and that is all an average means here.
answer_key.wrong: The story is read again with the total and the parts lit in turn, the bar is redrawn in equal parts, and the frame is replayed one digit at a time. Nothing is cleared and nothing is marked.

phase_mount.run: A phase is a complete activity in itself and it runs once. The teaching and the doing are not two screens and not two modes: the stage is furnished once, the voice talks over it, and the child starts working on the same stage without anything being rebuilt. Whatever the tool as a whole has to say goes into the FIRST phase's teach run, because there is no opening screen to say it on.
phase_mount.idle: NO AUTO-ADVANCE. After firing, the tool goes idle on the settled phase with the child's work still on it, and stops. Where the host supplies onNext it is drawn and it calls the host back; nothing in the component advances a phase.
phase_mount.prop: phase: number, 1-based, matching writeup.phases[].n. Rounded, clamped, and defaulting to 1 when the host sends nothing, so a bare mount is still a working tool rather than a blank screen. Read once: changing which phase a mount shows is a re-mount.
phase_mount.rule: ONE PHASE, ONE MOUNT. The host says which phase to build by passing `phase`, and the component builds that phase and nothing else. It does not know what came before it and it never moves on by itself.
phase_mount.opening: There is no opening panel and no Start button. The host has already chosen the activity, and a cover screen in front of it is a click between a child and the work. writeup.opening is the first frame of every mount rather than a panel of its own.
phase_mount.completion: The terminal event `finished`, with the phase in its detail, fired exactly once and guarded by a one-shot ref that only a restart re-arms, with the chime and the settle OUTSIDE the guard. props.onComplete is called alongside it: the event is the platform's signal and the callback is the host wrapper's, and firing only one of them leaves a child on a tool that never completes.
phase_mount.notInAMount: No finish card and no free play. Both are the host's now, built out of what the events told it. writeup.finish and writeup.freePlay stay as the record of what they are.

shared_state.note: What getState() returns. These names are a contract: the host reads them to persist and resume a child mid-activity, so renaming one breaks resume. `mode` is gone from this list because there is no mode. `phase` is the phase the host mounted, so a resume restores the work inside a phase and the host restores which phase.

agent_control.reason: Every tool in this chapter is child-operated. There is no agent-driven Concept mode, no postMessage command channel and no narration the tool waits on; the adult, where there is one, talks over the tool rather than through it.

steps: The whole distance, 456 km, is what is being shared, so it is the dividend.
It is shared equally among 24 litres, so 24 is the divisor.
456 divided by 24 is 19, since 24 times 19 is 456, so the van goes 19 km on one litre.
items.question: A van travels 456 km and uses 24 litres of petrol, and every litre carries it the same distance. How far does it go on one litre?
items.checkpoint: The total being shared is the dividend, and the number of equal parts is the divisor.
items.misconception: Trying to divide 24 by 456, which asks how much petrol one kilometre takes, a different question.

steps: The product and one number are known, so the other number is the product divided by the one you know.
294 tens divided by 32 is 9 tens, because 32 times 9 is 288, with 6 tens left.
64 ones divided by 32 is 2, so the other number is 92, and 32 times 92 is 2944.
items.question: Two numbers multiply to make 2944, and one of them is 32. What is the other?
items.checkpoint: A missing factor is the product divided by the factor you know.
items.misconception: Multiplying the two numbers given, as if the product were one of the factors.

steps: 49 hundreds divided by 24 is 2 hundreds, because 24 times 2 is 48, with 1 hundred left.
Bring down only the 6: 16 tens is smaller than 24, so 0 tens go in the quotient, with 16 tens left.
Now bring down the 8: 168 ones divided by 24 is 7, so the answer is 207, and 24 times 207 is 4968.
items.answer: The step for 16 tens was skipped. 16 tens is smaller than 24, so a zero goes in the tens place, and the answer is 207
items.question: A child works 4968 divided by 24, brings the 6 and the 8 down together, and gets 27. What step was skipped, and what is the right answer?
items.checkpoint: Bring down one digit at a time, and write a zero in the quotient whenever the number is smaller than the divisor.
items.misconception: Bringing two digits down at once and losing the zero, so 207 is read as 27.

steps: 4705 mL is shared into 15 equal parts, so divide 4705 by 15.
47 hundreds gives 3 with 2 left, 20 tens gives 1 with 5 left, and 55 ones gives 3 with 10 left.
The quotient, 313, answers how much is in each bowl, and the remainder, 10, answers how much is left: 15 times 313 is 4695, add 10 makes 4705.
items.answer: 313 mL in each bowl, and 10 mL left in the pot
items.question: A cook pours 4705 mL of soup equally into 15 bowls, as much as possible in each. How much is in each bowl, and how much is left in the pot?
items.checkpoint: When a question asks what is left, the remainder is part of the answer and cannot be dropped.
items.misconception: Giving only 313 and dropping the 10 mL, which is the answer to the second question.

learn.shape: Worked items, shown solved, mandatory before practice unlocks.
learn.selection: Fixed order, walking the phases from the first to the last.
learn.content_criterion: One per phase, so Learn walks the whole topic and stops.

items.question: A car park has 8 levels, and every level holds the same number of cars. It holds 3560 cars in all. How many does each level hold?
A child answers 18 questions in 54 minutes and spends the same time on each. How many minutes does each question take?
items.final_answer: 3 minutes, because 54 minutes shared among 18 questions is 3 each

items.question: Two numbers multiply to make 1386, and one of them is 42. Find the other.
1564 tiles are laid in 34 equal rows. How many tiles are in each row?
Two numbers multiply to make 6432, and one of them is 32. Find the other, and show the step that puts a zero in the quotient.
items.final_answer: 201. After 64 hundreds gives 2, the 3 tens come down, and 3 tens is smaller than 32, so a zero goes in the tens place of the quotient

items.question: A child divides 7560 by 36 and writes 21. Multiply back to test it, then correct it.
items.final_answer: 36 times 21 is 756, not 7560, so it is wrong. The last step divides 0 ones, which is smaller than 36, so a zero goes in the ones place: the quotient is 210

items.question: 5237 children are split equally into 25 teams for a sports day. How many are in each team, and how many are left out?
items.final_answer: 209 in each team and 12 left out. The quotient answers the first question and the remainder answers the second

items.question: A tailor cuts 2650 cm of cloth into 48 equal pieces, each as long as possible in whole centimetres. How long is each piece, and how much cloth is left?
items.final_answer: 55 cm each, with 10 cm left over, because 48 times 55 is 2640

practice.selection: Fixed order, easy first, and every phase represented.
practice.interaction_rules: Answered on the tool itself. A wrong answer returns the question with a hint; nothing is marked and retries are unlimited.

student_controls.effect: shows the story with its numbers lit, and lights the wording for each number's job
takes the number of equal parts
draws the total as a bar split into that many equal parts
holds a product and one of its numbers and divides to find the other
brings digits down singly and refuses two brought down together
lists each ask of the question with its own slot and its own unit

teaching_notes: Plan a trip on paper before the tool is opened: how many children, how many seats in a van, how many full vans, and how many children are left over. Then ask whether the answer to how many vans are needed is the quotient or one more than it. That question is the whole of this topic, because it makes the class decide what each part of a division means in the story. The opening page of the chapter asked how far a car goes on one litre, from the whole trip and the petrol used, and a box on this topic sends the child back to it to answer it now: the distance is shared among the litres, so it is the dividend. The worked example that finds a missing factor divides five thousand and seventy-five by twenty-five, and its figure brings the seven and the five down together. Seven tens is smaller than twenty-five, so a zero goes in the tens place; skip that step and the answer reads twenty-three instead of two hundred and three. The car park question assumes every level holds the same number of vehicles, which it does not say, so say it. The last two exercise questions each ask what is left, and there the remainder is an answer. The Critical Thinking box asks for the average time spent on each question and never says what an average is; here it means the time each question would take if every one took the same time. It also needs the time between two clock readings, which this chapter does not teach, so work that part out together first.
generation_prompt: Build a word problem tool on a fixed 1600x900 SVG stage. A story card sits across the top of the working area with each of its numbers lit. Under it wait a total slot and a parts slot; a number dragged from the story settles only in the slot whose job it does in that story, and a number dropped in the wrong slot springs back while the story's wording for that job is lit, with nothing marked. Once both are filled, a bar for the total is drawn and split into that many equal parts, and the division runs in a long division frame beside it. A missing factor bay holds a product and one of its two numbers, divides to build the other, and multiplies the two back to the product. The frame brings digits down one at a time and refuses two brought down together, so a step where the number is smaller than the divisor is always shown and its zero written in the quotient. An answer builder fixed down the right of the canvas lists each thing the question asks as its own slot with its own unit, such as kilometres for one litre, or children in each team and children left out, and it closes only when every slot is filled. Pointer events only, no assets, no network. Build it from the writeup and the tool build spec, not from this paragraph (maths_agent/TOOL_BUILD_SPEC.md). The three bands and every measurement come from writeup.stage and tool_config.style.stage: one header line, one canvas panel holding everything the child works on with the running count at its top left and the question, slot and pad fixed down its right as furniture, and a footer with the voice at the far left and the phase bar at the right. No sidebar, and no score box anywhere. One phase, one mount: build the phase the host passes and nothing else (tool_config.phase_mount). The first frame comes from writeup.opening. Each phase comes from writeup.phases, with its screen, action, reward and spoken line; its tries field is the hint ladder and its wrong list is what the stage does about a wrong answer, redrawn in steps on the working area with nothing marked and nothing reset. The one surprise is writeup.delight. The look and the sounds come from tool_config.style, voice and audio.
instructions_for_student: Find the number being shared. Find how many equal parts. Divide one digit at a time. Answer every question that is asked. Give each answer its unit.
